spatial_entity.notes: Analytical coastal/network frame for heterogeneous Swahili towns and maritime links. It is not one polity, one jurisdiction, a claim of uniform participation by every port, or a territorial-practice extent.

claim.date_text_original: near the 1400 horizon; thirteenth- and fourteenth-century maritime evidence with medieval specialist synthesis
claim.spatial_precision: analytical maritime/coastal network with heterogeneous nodes
claim.summary: Open specialist synthesis of Rasulid-Yemeni customs and shipping evidence describes regular thirteenth- and fourteenth-century trade linking Mogadishu and the southern Swahili coast to Arabia, with enslaved people among traded commodities. This supports a bounded external slave-trade-network participation claim around the 1400 horizon. It does not establish participation by every Swahili port, coast-wide territorial slavery, an exact network-wide volume, or a single Swahili political regime.

external_participation.role_text: Documented medieval maritime-network participation in movement/trade of enslaved people between parts of the Swahili coast and Arabian ports.
external_participation.notes: Network participation is analytically separate from territorial practice. Existing node-level evidence at Kilwa and Songo Mnara remains separate and must not be generalized to all coastlands or every network node.

source.title: When Did the Swahili Become Maritime?
source.geographic_scope: Swahili coast and western Indian Ocean
source.temporal_scope: first and second millennia CE, with explicit thirteenth- and fourteenth-century maritime evidence
source.independence_notes: Open specialist synthesis of archaeological and historical evidence. Its specific Rasulid/customs statements depend on underlying Yemeni source scholarship and are not treated as an independent primary archive.
source.reliability_limitations: Strong for regular maritime structure and the inclusion of enslaved people among traded commodities; it does not prove that every Swahili town or every voyage participated, nor does it quantify network-wide slave-trade volume.

evidence.evidence_role: near-anchor specialist synthesis of regular East Africa-Arabia maritime trade including enslaved people among traded commodities
evidence.directness: specialist synthesis citing Rasulid customs and late-fourteenth-century shipping evidence
evidence.locator: Background to Swahili archaeology; paragraph beginning 'explicit documentation of long-distance eastern African navigation', including Rasulid customs, Qadi Masud, and Kilwa-to-Aden evidence
evidence.notes: This is the principal claim-specific support for external/network participation; maritime connectivity by itself is not treated as slave-trade evidence.

source.title: Slave Trade and Urban Slavery on the Swahili Coast from Medieval Times to Abolition
source.independence_notes: Later specialist synthesis that overlaps earlier Swahili and Indian Ocean scholarship; not an independent direct event attestation.
source.reliability_limitations: Useful for classification and long-run scale/context, but the public publisher abstract alone does not provide port-by-port medieval proof and must not be used to infer uniform coast-wide prevalence.

geometry.resolution_method: No single point, route line, heritage boundary, or coast polygon can represent this mobile maritime network without implying false territorial or route completeness. Keep the network geometry unresolved. Kilwa, Songo Mnara, Tumbatu, and Mkokotoni may only be handled as separately reviewed node/evidence loci.
geometry.notes: The 100/100 geo numerator does not advance through this unresolved network geometry. Existing released Songo Mnara geometry and any future node loci remain separate case/evidence objects.
